britannica-1911-cappello-bianca:
Bianca Cappello (1548–1587) became grand duchess of Tuscany. She was born into a rich and noble Venetian family. Her great beauty was famous from her youth. This 1911 Britannica entry tells her dramatic story. At fifteen she fell in love with Pietro Bonaventuri. He was a young Florentine clerk with the Salviati firm. On 28 November 1563 she fled with him to Florence. They married there, and she bore a daughter, Pellegrina.

Venice tried hard to have Bianca arrested and returned. The grand duke Cosimo protected the couple instead. Her husband's poor family set her to menial work. Then her beauty caught Francesco, the grand duke's son. He was married already, to the Archduchess Giovanna. He took Bianca as his mistress and showered her with gifts. Her husband found court work and other comforts. In 1572 he was murdered in a Florence street. The entry hints that the lovers may have known of the deed.
britannica-1911-caravaca:
Caravaca is a town of south-eastern Spain. It stands in the province of Murcia. It lies near the left bank of the river Caravaca. That river is a tributary of the Segura. Its population in 1900 was 15,846. This 1911 Britannica entry describes the town and its shrine. The medieval castle of Santa Cruz dominates the place. Several convents stand within the town as well.

The parish church at Caravaca is a fine building. It holds a cross famed for healing power. A yearly festival honours that cross on 3 May. Crowds gather for the feast in spring. The hills to the north are rich in minerals. Marble and iron are both found there in quantity. The town has no railway link at all. Still, it works as a real industrial centre. Large iron-works and tanneries operate in the town. Paper, chocolate and oil are also made there.
britannica-1911-casablanca:
Casablanca is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a seaport on the Atlantic coast of Morocco, called Dar el Baida, “the white house,” in Arabic. It ranks third among the towns of the Moorish coast and serves as the wool and grain port for central Morocco. The roadstead has no bar or bad rocks but lies open to north west winds, and steamers anchor in five to six fathoms. Harbour works begun in May 1907 promised shelter at all tides.

Foreign trade through the port ran at about £750,000 a year across the decade 1897 to 1907. A railway to Ber Reshid opened in September 1908, the first railway built in Morocco. About 20,000 people lived in the town, among them many foreign merchants and a consular corps. The entry also recalls the Portuguese past: they built on the site of Anfa, a town they had destroyed in 1468, and later abandoned the place.
britannica-1911-confederate-states-of-am:
The Confederate States of America was the government formed by the seceding Southern states at the start of the American Civil War, in the winter of 1860 and 1861. Those states held roughly half the population of the North. In past national politics they had played a part past their share. Skilled statesmen, schooled in state politics and in Congress, framed the new union.

Jefferson Davis of Mississippi was the near-set choice for president. Alexander H. Stephens took the vice-presidency in his place. Stephens stood as a strong voice for states' rights. In war he became a sharp foe of Davis's use of power. Robert Toombs of Georgia, a strong secessionist, sat in the Confederate Congress. He too fought the grasping powers of the president. The long entry runs to war finance and home strain. Clever stand-ins for scarce goods, and fat profits from them, fill its middle pages.
britannica-1911-credit-mobilier-of-ameri:
The Crédit Mobilier of America was a construction company tied to the building of the Union Pacific Railroad. Its work gave rise to a grave political scandal in the United States Congress. Chartered in 1859 as the Pennsylvania Fiscal Agency, it fell under Thomas Durant's control in March 1864. Durant, a vice-president of the Union Pacific, renamed it and used it as the road's building arm.

Government and mortgage bonds paid the company slightly more than the whole cost of construction. A congressional report put its extra gains in stock and bonds at 23,000,000 dollars, a profit of about 48 percent. In 1872 letters made public showed that Oakes Ames had placed shares with members of Congress. The House censured Ames and James Brooks in 1873. A Senate committee urged the expulsion of James W. Patterson, but his term expired before any action was taken.
britannica-1911-foca:
Foca, pronounced Fawtcha, is a town of Bosnia set where the Drina and Cehotina rivers meet, ringed by wooded mountains. Its population in 1895 was 4,217. The town is headquarters of a thriving trade in silver filigree-work and inlaid weapons, for which it was famous. Its lands, enclosed by the frontiers of Montenegro and Novi Bazar, saw almost constant border warfare through the middle ages, when the town was known as Chocha.

No monuments of that age survive except the Bogomil cemeteries and the town's beautiful mosques, the oldest in Bosnia. Foca, Gorazda and Ustikolina were trading stations of the Ragusans in the fourteenth century. In the sixteenth century the Venetian ambassador Ramberti described it as Cozza, a large settlement of good Turkish-style houses, many shops and merchants. Through it all goods had to pass, and the governor of Herzegovina dwelt there.
britannica-1911-heidelberg-south-africa:
Heidelberg is a town and district of the Transvaal. The Vaal river bounds the district on the south. It includes the south-eastern Witwatersrand gold-fields. The town stands 42 miles south-east of Johannesburg. Durban lies 441 miles away by rail. Its population in 1904 was 3,220, of whom 1,837 were white. The town was founded in 1865. It is built on the Rand's slopes at 5,029 feet.

That elevation gives it a strong health reputation. It is reputed the best sanatorium in the colony. The town is the centre of the eastern Rand gold mines. The entry is a brief gazetteer notice. Position, population and founding year are its facts. The gold-fields and the sanatorium claim complete it. No church, history or trade detail is added.
britannica-1911-huancavelica:
Huancavelica is a city of central Peru and capital of a department, 160 m. S.E. of Lima. It stands in a deep ravine of the Andes, at about 12,400 ft. above the sea, the ravine averaging a mile wide. Its people were put at 6,000 in 1906. The city is solidly and regularly built of stone, and stone bridges span the stream that runs through it.

Near the city lies the famous quicksilver mine of Santa Barbara. Its church of San Rosario is hewn underground from the native cinnabar-bearing rock. Viceroy Francisco de Toledo founded Huancavelica in 1572 as a mining town, and mining remains the chief occupation of its people. The department, crossed by the Cordillera Occidental, held 167,840 people in 1906 over 9,254 square miles. The short account closes with its products and climate.
bundling-its-origin-progress-and-decline:
Henry Reed Stiles wrote a study of bundling, the old courtship custom, printed at Albany in 1871. A friend's sharp words set him to the work. Deacon Jabez H. Hayden had hit at a line on bundling in Stiles's History of Ancient Windsor. The hit, kind on both sides, drove a deep search of the point.

A Grant Thorburn line fronts the book: all writers agree, he says, that Yankees are a talking, guessing, swapping, and bundling folk. Start, spread, and fall of the custom form the book's three beats, as its title vows. Church, home, and court records of New England give the proof base. Stiles had form in town history — Brooklyn and Windsor both bear his name — and the same dig-and-cite hand runs this odd, small field. Shame, jest, and defence of New England's good name drive the pages.
burke-s-speech-on-conciliation-with-amer:
Burke's Speech on Conciliation with America presents Edmund Burke and his great parliamentary argument for settling with the American colonies, in an edition prepared for students by Sidney Carleton Newsom. Newsom, a teacher of English at Indianapolis, wrote the introduction for readers without a well stocked library, drawing on older editions and a bibliography he lists in full. The speech itself follows his framing chapters.

Contents pages lay out the study plan: the political situation, Burke as statesman, Burke in literature, topics for special reports, and then the speech with notes and an index. In the address, Burke urges Parliament to win the colonies back by concession rather than force, arguing from trade, distance, and the spirit of liberty in America. This printing serves the classroom: a classic piece of political persuasion, wrapped in the help a young reader needs to follow it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-africa:
Africa, a name of Phoenician origin, was first given by Romans to the territory around Carthage. It gradually spread to the whole Libyan territory Rome occupied. It was still understood in that sense in the eleventh century, when Leo IX wrote that after the Roman pontiff, Carthage's bishop stands first in Nubia and as Africa's chief metropolitan. Arabs then adopted the name, then medieval writers, until it came to cover the entire continent.

Africa spans about 12,000,000 square miles, about three times Europe and five times the United States without Alaska. It joins Asia only by the Suez Isthmus. Its shape is an irregular triangle, and its scarcity of bays and harbours seriously affected its history before steam. It rests on a rocky foundation forming an immense interior plateau, whence ranges like the Atlas branch off. The long entry moves from geography and peoples to missions and Islam.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-agostino-cias:
Agostino Ciasca, in the world Pasquale, was an Italian Augustinian cardinal, born at Polignano a Mare, in Bari province, on 7 May 1835. He died at Rome on 6 February 1902. He took the Augustinian habit in 1856, made profession in 1857, and was ordained priest in 1858. Having perfected himself at Rome in philosophy, theology, and canon law, he devoted himself particularly to Oriental languages, especially Arabic and Coptic.

Exemplary in life and loyal to the church, he became dear to Leo XIII, who gave him confidence and entrusted him with several delicate missions. In his order he served as professor, prefect of studies, assistant general, and procurator general. Later he served at the Vatican Council as theologian and interpreter for Oriental bishops. His chief works include Coptic-Sahidic biblical fragments from the Borgia Museum and Tatian's Arabic gospel harmony, edited with a Latin translation in 1888.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alvar-nunez-c:
Alvar Núñez Cabeza de Vaca, born at Jerez de la Frontera in Andalusia, has uncertain birth and death dates. His peasant family called themselves Alhaja until Las Navas de Tolosa, 1212. Turning the Arab position by a mountain pass, marked by a cow's skull, won them nobility. He joined Narváez's Florida expedition in 1526 as treasurer, one of four mainland survivors with two Spaniards and an Arab Moor.

Eight years roaming Louisiana and Texas coasts ended when his scant medicine and faith cures made him a renowned medicine man. After nine years they reached Sonora's Pacific coast, first Europeans across North America. He reached Mexico City in 1536, first European to see and describe the bison. La Plata governor from 1541, he was rebelled against in 1543, sent to Spain, and kept eight years in mild captivity. His Naufragios of 1542 and Comentarios of 1555 remain key sources.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ambrosian-bas:
The Ambrosian Basilica at Milan was raised by its great fourth-century bishop St. Ambrose and consecrated in the year 386. Its present form rose in four different periods, three in the ninth century and the fourth in the twelfth, though the original church is gone. Ambrose's own writings and modern research still give a fair idea of the founder's church. The original edifice resembled Rome's great churches of its age.

The basilica's story turns on Ambrose's final victory over the Arian court faction, after which the people sought its consecration.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-america:
America, the Western Continent or New World, holds three main divisions. North America runs from about 70 to 15 degrees north, Central America's isthmus narrows to thirty miles at Panama, and South America from 12 degrees north to 55 south. Animism underlies the Indian creed everywhere, fetishism its tangible form, and monotheism, a personal all-creating ruling God, nowhere existed. Five European nations chiefly settled the continent after Columbus: Spain, Portugal, France, England, and Holland in date order; Sweden's small colony lasted under seventeen years.

Spanish exploration's precious-metal mines were worked progressively through the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, then faded. The peoples later fought through the Napoleonic period to secure independence. No sufficient data fix America's Catholic population; even the United States' usual 14,000,000 is a conjecture more or less accurate.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-angelo-rocca:
Angelo Rocca founded Rome's Angelica Library. Born at Rocca, now Arcevia, near Ancona, in 1545, he died at Rome on 8 April 1620. At seven he was received into the Augustinian monastery at Camerino, hence also called Camers or Camerinus, and he studied at Perugia, Rome, and Venice. Padua made him a doctor in theology in 1577.

In 1579 he became secretary to the Augustinian superior-general, in 1585 he took charge of the Vatican printing office, and he supervised the planned Bible and Fathers' editions. He became sacristan in the papal chapel in 1595, and in 1605 titular Bishop of Tagaste in Numidia. Rome's Augustinian public library, formally established on 23 October 1614, keeps his name. Mainly through his efforts came the Vulgate edition published under Clement VIII. He also edited Egidio Colonna and Augustinus Triumphus, and wrote on the sacraments, Scripture, canonization, and bells.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apiarius-of-s:
Apiarius, a priest of Sicca in Roman Africa, matters in history only because his appeal to Rome sparked a long dispute between Rome and Carthage over who controls church discipline. Deposed by Urbanus, bishop of Sicca, for serious misconduct, he appealed to Pope Zosimus, who found flaws in the bishop's procedure, ordered the priest restored, and had the bishop disciplined. A general synod at Carthage in May 418 then forbade clerics below bishop to appeal beyond the seas, meaning across the Mediterranean to Rome.

Opponents of the papacy later read African resentment in the case as a denial of papal supremacy, the doctrine of the pope's supreme authority. Apiarius became the classic example in anti-Roman controversy for a fifth-century rejection of papal control. The article presents the case as a disciplinary quarrel that grew into a lasting argument about African church freedom and Roman claims.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-arca:
An arca was a box in which early Christians kept the Eucharist, the consecrated bread, in their homes. Cyprian tells of a woman who tried with unworthy hands to open her box holding the Lord's holy body. Fire issued from it the moment she touched it, and she could not open it. Wilpert believes a fresco in the catacomb of Saints Peter and Marcellinus shows such a box. It shows Christ seated reading from an open roll, three jars on his right, and on his left a square box filled with loaves, emblems of the Eucharist.

Arca also meant a receptacle for Christians' offerings for the church or the poor, cited from Tertullian and the Liber Pontificalis, the book of popes. The entry joins a devotional object and a charity chest under one Latin word, showing how early believers guarded the sacrament at home and gave for the common good.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-barca:
Barca was a titular see of Cyrenaica in northern Africa. Most archaeologists place it at Medinet el Merdja, though Graham puts it at Tolometa, or Tolmeita. Often destroyed and restored, it sank in the Roman period to a mere borough, yet still held a bishopric.

Its bishop Zopyros attended Nicaea in 325; Zephyrius is a mistaken form of his name. Zenobius and Theodorus appear in the subscriptions at Ephesus in 431 and Chalcedon in 451. Three bishops across three councils are all the record preserves. The see must have vanished when Arabs conquered the Pentapolis in 643.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bartholomew-o:
Bartholomew of Braganca was born about 1200 and died on 1 July 1271. Studying at Padua, he received the Dominican habit from St Dominic himself. In 1248 he was appointed to the Cypriot see of Nemonicum, a city now unknown. In 1254 he was sent as legate to England and France, following Henry III to Paris. There France's king gave him a relic of the true Cross and a thorn from the Crown.

Alexander IV made him Bishop of Vicenza in 1256, where he endured the tyranny of Ezzelino, religion's notorious enemy. The persecution drew out his high pastoral qualities, and he built Vicenza's Dominican Church of the Crown to house his relics. He joined King Louis of France at Joppa, Sidon, and Acre during the crusading expedition. Venerated by the people and honored as Blessed, he also wrote scriptural commentaries and sermons.

Bartholomew of Lucca was a historian born at Lucca about 1227, who died about 1327. Entering the Dominicans young, he won St Thomas Aquinas's respect and friendship as disciple, confidant, and confessor. In 1272 he followed Thomas from Rome to Naples, learning of his master's death at Fossa Nuova in 1274. He became prior of his native convent in 1288 and of Santa Maria Novella at Florence in 1301.

At Avignon he served nine years as chaplain to cardinals, and John XXII made him Bishop of Torcello in 1318. A clash with Grado's patriarch over an abbess brought excommunication and exile in 1321, but peace returned him in 1323. His best-known Annales, covering 1061 to 1303 in terse sentences, was finished about 1307. He verified statements with care, though his age's uncritical temper let fables like Popess Joan stand.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bartolommeo-p:
Bartolommeo Pacca was a cardinal, scholar, and statesman, born at Benevento in 1756, who died at Rome in 1844. Schooled by Jesuits at Naples and at Rome's Clementine College, he became nuncio at Cologne in 1785, a center of anti-Roman agitation. Consecrated titular Archbishop of Damiata, he arrived in June 1786 to find Cologne, Trier, and Mainz refusing recognition unless he renounced jurisdiction.

Other bishops and Cologne's magistrates received him respectfully, and even Prussia made no difficulty. Frederick William honored him on the Rhine, and Rome accorded the Prussian monarch the royal title. His Cologne position stayed difficult, as Bonn's new university preached open war on the Holy See. His memoirs record acute observations on politics and history, including his Cologne nunciature and the years 1809 to 1814.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-basilica:
Basilica is a word with two senses: a church's architectural style and its canonical status. In architecture it signifies a kingly, and secondarily beautiful, hall of Eastern origin, finest in Rome. Rome's Forum held basilicas of Porcia, Fulvia, Sempronia, and Opimia between 184 and 121 BC, then Caesar's Basilica Julia after 46 BC. They beautified the Forum and served markets and justice, open to the public and well lighted.

Vitruvius gives the usual plan: a parallelogram whose width runs between a third and a half of its length. Columns divide the middle space from a lower ambulatory as wide as the columns are high, with shorter upper columns admitting light. Canonically, basilica rank brings precedence over other churches, save the local cathedral, plus the conopaeum, bell, and cappa magna. The conopaeum, a red and yellow silk umbrella, is carried with the bell at the clergy's head on state occasions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cardica:
Cardica was a titular see of Thessaly, the Latinized medieval form of Gardicium, truly Gardikion in Greek. It appears only in later see-lists from the 1100s or 1200s, under Larissa. Lequien names five Latin bishops from 1208 to 1389, beginning with Bartholomew, recipient of many letters from Pope Innocent III.

Lequien knew no Greek bishop of the see, but manuscript lists add eight names. They run from John in 1191 to Gregorius about 1852, with Metrophanes degraded in 1623 and Sophronius serving from 1646 to 1649. When Thessaly joined Greece in 1881 the see had stood vacant since 1875. It was suppressed in 1899, and Gardiki survives as a small town of about 3,000 people in the diocese of Phthiotis.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-catholic-knig:
The Catholic Knights of America was a fraternal life-insurance company chartered under Kentucky law. Four Nashville men founded it. James J. McLoughlin led the group. D. N. Burke joined him, as did John Broderick and John McDonald. They first met on 23 April 1877 at Emmett Hall. The society began as the Order of United Catholics and later took its new name at Bishop P. A. Feehan's suggestion. Feehan, of Nashville, became its spiritual director.

Growth was rapid: sixteen branches met in the first supreme council at Louisville in July 1878, and seventy-two were represented at Indianapolis the next year. By 1 August 1907 the order counted 20,000 members in 560 branches across forty-two states. It had paid nearly fifteen million dollars to heirs of over 8,500 deceased members, and held resources of $828,000.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-catholic-univ:
The Catholic University of America is a pontifical institution in Washington, D.C., comprising schools of Sacred Sciences, Philosophy, Law, Letters, and Science. Supreme authority rests with the Holy See, while governing power lies with the bishops of the United States, exercised through a board of trustees of bishops, priests, and laymen. The Archbishop of Baltimore serves as chancellor ex officio, and a rector, aided by an academic senate, runs the university day to day.

The desire for such a university was voiced at the Second Plenary Council of Baltimore in 1866 and took definite shape at the Third in 1884. By 1907 the university counted 32 teachers and 210 students, with a library of 100,000 volumes and its own quarterly, The Catholic University Bulletin.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-clerks-regula:
The Clerks Regular of the Mother of God of Lucca were founded by Blessed Giovanni Leonardi, born in 1541 at Diecimo in the Republic of Lucca. Sent to Lucca at seventeen to learn the apothecary's trade, he was piously inclined from childhood and was ordained on 22 December 1572. His congregation began in 1574, when two or three young laymen gathered round him for guidance in reforming manners and saving souls.

When his lay helpers prepared for priesthood and a religious order took shape, persecution broke out. The Fathers of the republic feared a native order spreading over Italy would expose the little state's affairs. Persecution kept Leonardi mostly banished from Lucca, admitted only by special Senate decree under papal pressure. In 1580 he secretly acquired Santa Maria Cortelandini, still held by his sons. Bishop Guidiccioni canonically erected the congregation in 1583 at Gregory the Thirteenth's instigation, confirmed by Clement the Eighth's brief of 13 October 1595.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-concordia-in-:
Adolphus Ennis's entry covers the Diocese of Concordia in northwestern Kansas. Erected on 2 August 1887, it borders Colorado west, Nebraska north, and county lines east and south, across 26,685 square miles. In 1886 Leavenworth split into three sees: Leavenworth, Wichita, and Concordia. Richard Scannell of Nashville, nominated first bishop on 9 August 1887, ruled until 30 January 1891, when he moved to Omaha. Wichita's bishop then administered Concordia, and no new bishop came until 1897.

Growth followed fast. From 1898 to 1907, forty-five churches and twenty schools rose, besides new missions and stations. An 1884 boarding school for young ladies under the Sisters of Saint Joseph had led the way. By the time of writing, fifty-one secular and fifteen religious priests served ninety-one churches, thirty stations, and four chapels. Parochial schools held about 2,482 children, and academies at Concordia and Abilene about 135 pupils. The Catholic population stood at 26,125.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-corsica:
Alexandre Guasco's entry covers Corsica, the Mediterranean's third island in size, surpassed only by Sicily and Sardinia. Antibes on the French Riviera lies one hundred and eleven miles from Calvi, Corsica's port nearest France. Brisk commerce runs between Leghorn in Italy and Bastia in Corsica, the voyage taking five hours. The island is mountainous and well watered, largely covered with forests and almost impenetrable thickets called maquis.

Coastal climate stays mild, while elevated regions run cold. Corsica's area measures 3,367 square miles, its population 300,000. Interior and coastal natives alike, descended from Italians, are nearly all Catholics. Phoenicians and Phocians early visited the island and established colonies there. For a time it belonged to Carthage. Christianity, it has been asserted, entered Corsica in Apostolic times. Before and after 600 the island stood in close dependence on the Apostolic See, and always remained so.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-council-of-sa:
The Council of Sardica, held most probably in 343, belongs to the series of councils wrestling with Arian doctrine and its fallout. Emperors Constans and Constantius convoked it at Pope Julius's urging, choosing Sardica, now Sofia, for a genuinely representative meeting. Athanasius and other bishops, condemned and vindicated by turns, awaited a final judgment.

Eastern bishops, in the minority, withdrew to act as a body, while the remainder refused to add to the Nicene Creed and enacted canons on bishops' transfers, trials, and appeals. Documents went to Pope Julius with a majority letter, yet pacification failed entirely, and the Eastern bishops grew bolder in defiance.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cuenca:
A diocesan entry describes Cuenca, a suffragan see of Quito in Ecuador, created in 1779. Its episcopal city, 7,700 feet above sea level in a broad plain south-east of Guayaquil, holds 30,000 people, with Peruvian antiquities nearby. The diocese covers Azuay and Canar, and ranks second among Ecuadorian sees.

Jesuits led the first missions, followed by Franciscans, Dominicans, and others, working 130 successful years until the Society's expulsion in 1767. A Salesian mission now works eastward in Gualaquiza. The Franciscan Vicente Solano, famed as a controversialist, belonged to this diocese. Its organization owes most to Bishop Toral, who served from 1861 to 1883 and attended the Vatican Council.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cuernavaca:
A church entry covers Cuernavaca, set up in 1891 for the whole state of Morelos in Mexico. It is bounded by the archdioceses of Mexico and Puebla and the bishopric of Chilapa. It spans 7,184 square kilometres with 161,697 people, served in 34 parishes by 42 diocesan and 6 order priests.

Franciscans first preached the Gospel here, founding the Cuernavaca convent in 1526. Dominicans followed at Oaxtepec in 1529, and Augustinians at Ocuituco in 1534. By 1536, the Franciscan writer Motolinia claims, all the people had turned to the Faith. In the 1700s most churches passed from the orders to diocesan clergy. The first bishop, Fortino Hipolito Vera, was consecrated in 1894 and died four years later.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dacca:
A diocesan entry traces Dacca, a see in Bengal, India, from Portuguese jurisdiction to its own hierarchy. By a constitution of Paul III in 1534, Goa held spiritual rule from the Cape of Good Hope as far as China. Bengal's early Portuguese settlements fell under Goa. From 1606 they fell under Mylapore.

When British rule replaced Portugal, Mylapore still kept jurisdiction, and 7,000 of Dacca's 22,000 Catholics remained subject to it. For effective mission work, Propaganda made a Jesuit vicar apostolic of Calcutta and Bengal in 1834. Pius IX divided Bengal into two vicariates in 1850. A third followed in 1870. On the creation of the Indian hierarchy in 1886, the eastern vicariate rose to the Diocese of Dacca.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-diego-alvarez:
Diego Alvarez Chanca served as court physician to the Spanish sovereigns Ferdinand and Isabella. He sailed with Christopher Columbus on his second voyage to America in 1493. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry credits him with treating Columbus through a bout of malarial fever soon after landing in Haiti. He also saved other leaders of the expedition who fell sick.

On ground Chanca himself chose, the settlers raised Isabella, the first Christian town in the New World. It was named for the queen. His letter to the council of his home city, written after only three months on shore, stands as the first account of American plants, animals, and peoples.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-domenico-capr:
Domenico Capranica was a cardinal, theologian, canonist, and statesman, born near Palestrina in 1400. At Padua and Bologna he studied canon and civil law brilliantly, winning the doctorate of both laws at twenty-one. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry follows him as secretary to Martin the Fifth and apostolic prothonotary, made cardinal in secret in 1423 or 1426, though his rank was not proclaimed until 1430.

He earned swift rise by political and military service, ruling Imola and Forli and winning back rebellious Bologna. He became bishop of Fermo and played a part at the Council of Basle, of which he is said to have written a history never printed. His Rules of Life for a nephew, the entry notes, mirror a fine character. He died at Rome in 1458.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fabriano-and-:
Fabriano and Matelica form one diocese in central Italy, in the province of Macerata. Fabriano is famed for paper works and salted-fish trade. It is said to descend from refugees of ancient Attidium in the ninth century before Christ. Its baptismal font stayed at Attigio until 1254. Its story runs with the Marches.

San Benedetto holds the tomb of Blessed Giovanni Bonnelli, dead in 1290. Saint Silvestro Guzzoli, founder of that order, lies at Monte Fano nearby, and the relics of Saint Romuald moved to Saints Biagio and Romoaldo in 1480. Fabriano stood under Camerino until 1785, when Pius VI restored Matelica and joined it to Fabriano as equal heads. Matelica was a Roman colony from 89 before Christ, and its ancient bishops Equitius and Florentius are named. Gentile da Fabriano, the painter, was its most famed native.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-german-roman-:
The German Roman Catholic Central Verein of North America united German Catholic benevolent societies against secret societies and for Catholic rights. Its origin lies in 1854, when presidents of three Buffalo societies called German Catholic bodies together, urged by missionary priests and approved by Bishop Timon. A Mainz union of 1848 lent the model, and seventeen societies organized the Verein at Baltimore's Saint Alphonsus Hall on April 15, 1855.

Membership stayed limited to German-language Catholic benevolent societies, growing from seventeen societies and 1,500 members in 1855 to 548 societies and 48,989 members in 1895. A 1901 reorganization replaced direct local affiliation with state associations, and by 1907 sixteen state bodies and fifty-two locals counted 99,291 paid-up members. Pius IX praised the Verein in 1866, its fifty-two years gave about twelve thousand dollars to Peter's Pence, and its immigrant agents and Leo House in New York served newcomers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gioacchino-ve:
Gioacchino Ventura di Raulica was an Italian pulpit orator, patriot, and philosopher born at Palermo in 1792, who died at Versailles in 1861. He entered the Jesuits in 1808 and, when the order was suppressed in Sicily, joined the Theatines in 1817. Leo XII made him professor of canon law at the Sapienza, and in 1830 he became Superior-General of the Theatines. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows his preaching and his politics in turn.

His eloquence, vehement and direct with a magnificent voice, won him renown in Rome and Paris, where he almost rivaled Lacordaire. Under Pius IX he glorified the union of religion and liberty. He defended the Sicilian Revolution, dreaming of an Italian confederation under the pope. After the Roman Republic fell in 1849 he withdrew to France, preached before Napoleon III, and closed his life as a moderate Traditionalist philosopher.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giovanni-batt:
Giovanni Battista de Luca was a cardinal and Italian canonist of the seventeenth century, born at Venosa in southern Italy in 1614, who died at Rome in 1683. Born of humble parents, he studied at Naples, returned home in ill health, and went to Rome in 1645. There his legal skill won him a high reputation, along with much envy. A Catholic Encyclopedia article presents a practical jurist of the Roman court.

Late in life he became a priest under the patronage of Innocent XI, who made him referendary, auditor of the Sacred Palace, and finally cardinal in 1681. His writings matter most for understanding the jurisprudence of the Roman court and the Rota of his day. His complete works, the Theatrum veritatis et justitiae, ran to nineteen volumes, with a later Cologne edition in twelve.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-greek-catholi:
Greek Catholics in America is an article on the Uniat churches of the Byzantine or Greek Rite, almost unknown in the United States some twenty-five years before 1909. Occasional priests from Syria came seeking aid, but their rite and peoples were wholly unknown to American Catholics. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows the Slav immigration that changed that picture.

Emigration from the Slav lands of Austro-Hungary brought the Greek Rite in large numbers, with churches erected all over the country. The movement began about 1879 to 1880. Coal companies in Pennsylvania, terrorized by the Molly Maguires from 1871 to 1879, sought foreign labor abroad. The Austrian Slav, willing to work longer hours for less, succeeded in wage-earning, and his countrymen followed into the coal and iron districts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-greek-orthodo:
The Greek Orthodox Church in America is an article on those of the Greek Rite not in communion with the Holy See. Both sides share the official designation, but the dissenting churches stress Orthodox, correctness of doctrine, while the Uniat churches stress Catholic. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows seven nationalities without unity or central obedience.

Nearly every city of size holds one or more churches of the communion. They conform to Byzantine usages but look to home Holy Synods for government. Seven nationalities use Old Slavonic, Greek, Arabic, and Rumanian as liturgical languages, and the Russian is the oldest and best established. Russian monks reached Alaska in 1793, built the first church on Kodiak Island in 1794, and converted many Eskimo and Indians before Alaska's sale in 1867.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-huesca:
Huesca is a Spanish diocese in north-eastern Spain, covering parts of Huesca province, seven parishes in the Broto valley, and three parishes near Saragossa. Its origin cannot be fixed for certain: the earliest sure evidence is Bishop Gabinius signing Toledo's council decrees in 589. Isidore of Seville mentions an earlier bishop, Elpidius, but that testimony counts as less authoritative.

A synod at Huesca in 598 ordered yearly diocesan conferences and disciplinary measures. The Moorish invasion reached Huesca by 710, the city fell in 713, and the bishop fled, with the diocese run from Aragon. In 1063 the see moved to Jaca, staying there until Huesca was retaken in 1096 and Pedro I restored the original see. Later history ties Huesca closely to Barbastro, erected from its territory in 1571.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hungarian-cat:
Hungarian Catholics in America came from a kingdom whose people were far from all Magyar. The Kingdom of Hungary, separate from Austria except for foreign affairs, held Slovaks, Ruthenians, Rumanians, Slavonians, Croatians, Germans, and Italians alongside Hungarians proper, who barely formed a majority against all others combined. Immigrants from that kingdom were thus indiscriminately called Hungarians in America.

This article treats only immigrants of Hungarian race and language in the Roman rite, leaving Greek-rite Hungarians and other races to other articles. Their settlements lay scattered, usually in small numbers far apart, with only New York, Cleveland, Chicago, and Bridgeport large enough to support a church and priest. Magyar priests for mission work proved extremely hard to find, and dioceses tried various means to supply the lack.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hydatius-of-l:
Hydatius of Lemica, also called Idatius, was a chronicler and bishop. His birthplace was Lemica in Galicia, Ginzo de Limia in Spain today, late in the fourth century, and he died shortly after 468. As a child on a journey to Jerusalem he met St. Jerome. He entered clerical life around 417, and consecration as bishop followed in 427, probably for Aquae Flaviae, modern Chaves in Portugal.

Hydatius wielded political influence, shown when he went to Aëtius in Gaul in 431 to seek help against the Suevi. His Chronicle continues Jerome's work from 379 to 468. For its first part he draws on others' testimony, but from 427 onward he writes as a contemporary witness. Whether he also wrote the Fasti Consulares for 245 to 468, appended to the Chronicle, remains doubtful.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-isidore-of-th:
Cardinal Isidore of Thessalonica, sometime metropolitan of Kiev, was born near the end of the fourteenth century and died at Rome on 27 April 1463. He ranked among the chief Eastern champions of reunion with Rome at the Council of Florence. His birth date is unknown and his people uncertain — described as Bulgar by some and Greek by others — though all his schooling was Greek.

At Constantinople he became a monk and abbot of St Demetrius. He was a man of unusually complete learning. He was strong in Latin, famed as a theologian, and a skilled orator. He was eager for reunion from the start. Constantinople, facing ruin by the Turks, weighed rescue by Western princes as the price of reunion, and in 1434 Isidore was sent to Basel. The entry follows a Greek churchman betting his career on East-West unity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jaca:
Jaca stands in Spain's Huesca province, chief town of the Sobrarbe mountains. It lies on the Aragon river, a tributary of the Ebro. It sits about 2,400 feet above sea level. It was once capital of the Jaccetani tribe named by Strabo. Its land saw battles between Sertorius and Pompey. Later it saw fighting between Pompey's son and Caesar's generals.

In church terms Jaca first belonged to Huesca's diocese. When Moors seized Huesca in 713, wandering bishops served the region. They lived at Jaca or in nearby monasteries. A council at Jaca in 1063 redrew Huesca's diocesan bounds. Those bounds later covered the present Huesca dioceses. The entry pairs mountain geography with a shifting church map.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jamaica:
Jamaica, the largest British West Indian island, lies in the Caribbean Sea. It sits 90 miles south of Cuba and 100 miles west of Haiti. It lies 554 miles from Colon. The nearest mainland point is about 400 miles southwest. Its name is said to come from Arawak words for water and wood, meaning a fertile land. The island runs 144 miles long and 21 to 49 miles broad.

Its area is 4,207 square miles, of which about 646 are flat alluvium, marl, and swamp. Copper is its most abundant mineral. The surface is very mountainous, with almost 2,000 square miles above 1,000 feet. Blue Mountain Peak rises 7,360 feet. Over two thousand plant and animal species are noted. The entry then covers history, peoples, government, and Catholic life on a sugar island of striking contrasts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jose-ribeiro-:
José Ribeiro da Fonseca was a Portuguese Franciscan friar who rose to lead his order and then a diocese. Born at Evora in 1690, he joined the Franciscans at Ara Coeli in Rome in 1712. As minister general, the order's worldwide head, he worked to restore discipline where it had grown lax, with a care praised for prudence and tact.

He founded a large library in the old Ara Coeli convent in 1740 and backed the Rome publication of Wadding's Annales Minorum in seventeen volumes between 1731 and 1741. Though he several times refused a bishopric, he at last accepted Oporto in 1741 on the nomination of King John V of Portugal.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lipsanotheca:
Lipsanotheca is a church term for the small box that holds relics, the sacred remains or belongings of a saint. People sometimes use the word for the whole reliquary, the larger shrine in which relics are shown, but the entry draws a sharp line between the two.

Strictly, the lipsanotheca is the inner case, tucked inside the outer shrine. Knowing the split matters for anyone reading old church inventories or guides to shrines, where the two words can look alike yet point to different objects, one held within the other.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lucca:
Lucca is an archdiocese and Tuscan city on the Serchio, in a fertile plain famed for marble, silk, wool, flax, hemp, and olive oil known worldwide. Its cathedral, sixth-century in origin, was rebuilt in Roman style in the eleventh century and consecrated by Alexander II in 1070.

Civitali's St. Martin, Pisano's Deposition, and Giovanni da Pisa's Adoration grace the facade, with Tintoretto and Fra Bartolommeo inside. Most famed is the Volto Santo, an old wooden crucifix in a long sleeveless robe, carried as a palladium by travelling Lucchesi and seeding legends of St. Wilgefortis. Eighty churches, the ducal palace, and a rich library complete the picture.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-malacca:
Malacca was a diocese covering the southern Malay Peninsula, then called the Straits Settlements. Its range ran from Singapore and Penang down through Selangor, Perak, and Kelantan. It stretched some 400 miles north to south. Though outside India, it answered to Pondicherry as suffragan.

About 28,000 Catholics lived among roughly 1,800,000 people. Forty-two priests of the Paris Foreign Missions served them in 57 churches and chapels. The cathedral of the Good Shepherd stood at Singapore. A college for native clergy stood at Penang. Forty-nine schools taught 6,660 children. Paul IV erected the see in 1557 under Portuguese patronage. Jurisdiction passed to Ava and Pegu in 1838, then to Siam in 1840. Leo XIII revived it as a diocese in 1888. Edouard Gasnier was its first bishop, followed by Rene Fee and then Emil Barrilon.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mecca:
Mecca, capital of Arabia and sacred city of Islam, lies in the Hijaz district some seventy miles east of the Red Sea. It sits in a sandy valley ringed by rocky, barren hills two hundred to five hundred feet high. Birthplace of Mohammed and home of the Kaaba, it was famed even before Islam as the Arabs' chief sanctuary, drawing pilgrims and devotees from afar.

The town looks fairer than most Eastern towns, with broad streets and stone houses, usually three stories, well aired and lit. Its some 60,000 people, nearly all Arabs, live chiefly by lodging pilgrims and serving the temple, with trade to desert Bedouins besides. Once seat of government under the first five caliphs, it is now ruled by a Sharif drawn from Mohammed's descendants, under the Turkish sultan. Some 80,000 pilgrims visit each year, passing Medina on the way.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-minorca:
Minorca, suffragan of Valencia, comprises the island of Minorca, second in size of the Balearic Islands, Spanish possessions. The civil capital is Port Mahon and the ecclesiastical capital Ciudadela. The diocese's origin is unknown, but it certainly existed in the fifth century, since its bishop Macarius, with Elias and Opilio of Majorca, took part in the events of that age.

Later, under Moorish rule, the island's Christians endured centuries of obscurity. The article recounts the expedition, directed by a certain Theodore, to convert the Jews who held Minorca, and the even more famous letter of Bishop Severus describing mass conversions in 418. After the Christian reconquest the see was restored, and Ciudadela became its seat, a role it has kept through Minorca's changing masters.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-oaxaca:
Oaxaca, an archdiocese in southern Mexico also called Antequera, ranks fourth among the first sees of the Americas. Paul III erected it on 21 July 1535, after Tlaxcala, Mexico, and Guatemala, and Leo XIII raised it to an archbishopric in 1891 with Chiapas, Yucatán, Tabasco, Tehuantepec, and Campeche beneath it.

Before the conquest its peoples worshipped sun, moon, stars, and ancestors, yet missionaries converted thousands and built churches across the region. Only thirty bishops had ruled the see by the entry's date, the last being Eulogio Gillow, preconized in 1887. Cortes sought Tlaxcalan aid against Moctezuma, and gratitude shaped the first American bishoprics.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-orange-river-:
The Orange River vicariate, also called Great Namaqualand, serves a desert coastland of South Africa from the Atlantic to the Kalahari. Erected as a vicariate in 1897 after serving as a prefecture since 1885, it covers Little Namaqualand, Bushmanland, and districts east to Gordonia beyond the river.

For thirty to a hundred miles inland the land is sandy desert, living only on thunderstorms, yet a good rain wakes rich pasture overnight. A prefecture split off in 1909 covers Great Namaqualand north to Damaraland, with Rehoboth as its town, and the entry lists missions and priests.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pedro-abarca:
Pedro Abarca was a theologian born in Aragon in 1619 and dead on 1 October 1693 at Palencia. He entered the Society of Jesus in 1641 and spent almost all his religious life as professor of scholastic, moral, and controversial theology, chiefly at Salamanca University. Though Hurter's Nomenclator omits him, he left many theological works.

Chief among them are five quarto volumes on the Incarnation and Sacraments, one quarto volume on Grace, and several lesser treatises on moral and dogmatic subjects. He also wrote widely on history: Historical Annals of the Kings of Aragon and The First Kings of Pampeluna, besides many manuscripts and one withheld work about the Church of del Pilar.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pedro-caldero:
Pedro Calderon de la Barca, born 1600 and dead 1681, was a Spanish dramatist whose work marks Spain's golden age's second half. His age was one of social decay under Philip III and Philip IV. All signs pointed to loss of the empire Spain had won. Yet even then Spain produced a poet of weight in Calderon.

His value has been overrated, since the modern world let him outshine Lope de Vega, though Calderon inherited stage traditions Lope had developed. Yet Calderon interpreted those traditions in a way that captivated his contemporaries as it did Germany's later Romantics. By giving full voice in theatre to national qualities, he endeared himself to his people. That bond will guard his repute wherever Spanish is spoken and Spain's past glory is revered. Of northern Asturian stock, though born at Madrid, he trained in the capital, then spent six years at Salamanca University.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pedro-da-fons:
Pedro da Fonseca was a philosopher and theologian born at Cortizada in 1528, dead at Lisbon in 1599. He joined the Jesuits in 1548. In 1551 he moved to Evora, lecturing so subtly and brilliantly as to earn the name Portuguese Aristotle.

His works were used in Europe's schools for a century. They are his Dialectical Institutions, Lisbon 1564, his Metaphysics commentaries, Rome 1577, and his Philosophical Introduction, Lisbon 1591. These works appeared in many editions from Catholic press. Fonseca also shares fame for the Conimbricenses, since as provincial, by his initiative, Coimbra's Jesuits undertook that work. As a man of affairs he matched his philosophy. He served as assistant for Portugal to the general, visitor of Portugal, and superior of Lisbon's house. Gregory XIII and Philip II employed him in affairs of delicacy and consequence. He used his influence for charity and learning. Many Lisbon institutions, the Irish college among them, owe existence to him.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-de-mar:
Pierre de Marca was a French bishop and scholar, born at Gan in Béarn on 24 January 1594. After letters at Auch and law at Toulouse, he became councillor of Pau's parliament in 1615, president in 1621, and intendant of Béarn in 1631. There he helped restore Catholicism almost extinguished under Jeanne d'Albret. His wife died in 1631, leaving four children, and he gave spare hours to history and canon law.

Summoned to Paris's Council of State in 1639, he published Concordia sacerdotii et imperii in 1641 at Richelieu's request, setting out Gallican views. Made Bishop of Couserans in 1641, he waited ten years for preconization after his book reached the Index and he retracted. As intendant of French Catalonia from 1644 he wrote Marca Hispanica, published posthumously by Baluze. Archbishop of Toulouse in 1652, he pressed acceptance of Innocent X's condemnation of Jansenism, and, after Cardinal de Retz resigned, received Paris, dying about three weeks after preconization in 1662.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-portugues-eas:
Portuguese East Africa is the Province of Mozambique. Work on that coast began in 1505 with the Captaincy of Sofala. A fortress rose at Mozambique in 1558, a port of call for India ships and a base for pushing inland. From it, explorers overran the native empire of Monomotapa in search of gold. Ruled from Goa for centuries, the lands became a government of their own in 1752, though rule long reached little beyond the coast.

The 1891 Anglo Portuguese Treaty settled a boundary quarrel with England and cut the province down. It still holds 1,428 miles of coast, from Cape Delgado to the south end of the Lourenço Marques district, and 292,631 square miles. The coast runs low, with reefs, dunes, and swamps, under a hot, unhealthful climate. Lourenço Marques, the best harbour in south east Africa, links by rail to the Transvaal, and Beira serves the Mashona gold fields.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-portuguese-we:
Portuguese West Africa usually names the Province of Angola. Its coast runs 1,015 miles from the Congo to the Cunene, and its area is 490,525 square miles, counting Cabinda, Molendo, and Massabi north of the Congo. Diego Cam entered the Congo in 1484 and raised a pillar as a mark of occupation, with Martin Behaim beside him. Save for Dutch rule from 1640 to 1648, it stayed Portuguese.

The coast runs low, with a sandy, barren plain reaching some way inland. Past it the land rises mountainous and very fertile. The capital, St Paul de Loanda, holds a 1,700-acre anchorage. Benguella, Mossamedes, and Porto Alexandre count as good ports. Lobito, end of the new railway, lacks drinkable water. Its chief wealth is coffee, rubber, gum, wax, and ivory, traded for cotton and woollen goods and wine. Once its wealth rested almost wholly on the slave trade to Brazil.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pre-columbian:
Of all claimed finds of America ere Columbus, only the Vikings' sails to Greenland and the mainland count as sure history. Tales of Phoenician, Irish, Welsh, and Chinese finds rest on word too vague to defend. The oldest written word comes from Adam, a canon of Bremen, who about 1067 took up Norse history there. Adam also drew on King Sven Estrithson, who held the whole tale of the northern folk in mind as if graven.

Adam names only Greenland and Vineland among lands the Northmen found. Greenland he calls an isle about as far from Norway as Iceland. Dig and old lore fix the settlements, their churches, houses, and manors, and the size and life of the Norse folk. Churches ran fifty to sixty five feet long and twenty six wide. The Gripla counts twelve churches in the east settlement and four in the west.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-prefecture-ap:
This Grisons canton prefecture in Switzerland holds the Moesa valley and the Calanca valley. The Moesa starts at the San Bernardino pass and runs to the Ticino. The Calancasca flows through Calanca. Its folk number 6,027, of whom 6,011 are Catholic, 5,945 of them Italians. Misocco chapter holds 8 parishes, 5 Capuchins, and 4 secular priests. Calanca holds 11 parishes served by 5 Capuchins and 3 seculars.

At Misocco, called Mesocco in Italian, stands a canonry led by a prior with six canons. Three live in Misocco, three in San Vittore. Roveredo holds St Anna's Catholic Institute, under Piccola Casa della Providenza's Fathers. The prefecture rose in 1635 at Bishop Joseph Mohr of Chur's wish, on whose urging Propaganda sent Capuchin missioners to the Italian speaking folk of the two valleys. Capuchins from Milan came first, then Novara, then Pavia, and since 1850 the Capuchins of Ticino.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-republic-of-c:
Costa Rica is a narrow isthmus between Panama to the east and Nicaragua to the north, with the Caribbean Sea on the north-east and the Pacific on the south-west. It covers 18,400 square miles, with a 1905 population of 334,307 besides 3,500 Indians. San José, the capital, holds 24,500 people, then Cartago 7,800 and Heredia 7,151. Two ports stand on the Atlantic coast and two on the Pacific, and mountain chains cross the land in many directions.

The principal chain runs the whole length from north-west to south-east, rising to Pico Blanco at 11,800 feet. Six partly active volcanoes break the skyline, the tallest, Irazu, at 11,600 feet, dormant. On the church side, the bishop of León in Nicaragua administered Costa Rica until 1850. In 1908 Pius the Tenth restored the Apostolic delegation, naming Giovanni Cagliera, titular Archbishop of Sebaste, envoy-extraordinary and delegate, at the republic's welcome.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-monica:
Monica of Tagaste, mother of Augustine, was born of Christian parents in North Africa in 333 and died at Ostia near Rome in 387. Married young to Patritius, a pagan official of violent temper and loose habits, she lived an unhappy married life, yet won his respect through patience and prayer. Her entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia tells how a mother's endurance shaped a great convert.

By sweetness rather than scolding she became a guide to other wives in Tagaste who suffered as she did. Three children were born to the marriage, Augustine the eldest, and her long prayers for his conversion became the best-known part of her story. She died on the journey home after Augustine's baptism, and the entry keeps its focus on the household faith that steadied him.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-salamanca:
Salamanca, a Spanish diocese covering the civil provinces of Salamanca, Cáceres, Avila, and León, borders Portugal on the west and Zamora, Avila, Valladolid, and Cáceres on its other sides. Its cathedral city counted 23,000 people, and Roman Salamanca left a bridge of twenty-seven arches over the Tormes, five hundred paces long and probably built under Trajan. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia traces a see of unknown origin.

Tradition places its founding just after the apostles, and bishops of Salamanca sign the councils of Toledo, from Eleutherius at the third to Egeretus at the seventh, eighth, and tenth. The entry then follows the diocese through Moorish and Christian centuries to its university fame and modern state. Readers get the geography, the Roman roots, and the long roll of bishops in one compact survey.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-san-jose-de-c:
San José de Costa Rica, a diocese covering the whole republic as suffragan of Guatemala, was established in 1850, and by 1910 its Catholic population of 368,000 matched nearly the entire country. The republic counted 103 priests, sixty-eight parish churches, ninety-eight chapels, one seminary, one diocesan college, one girls' academy, two orphan asylums, and four hospitals, all church-supported. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia is a census of a Catholic nation.

At the capital, the seminary held ten students and the diocesan college 150 pupils. The Sisters of Our Lady of Sion ran an academy with thirty-five sisters and a hundred girls, plus a poor girls' school of eighty. Sisters of Charity cared for 230 orphans in San José, and Salesians kept another asylum for 233 at Cartago. The entry also notes President Castro's 1847 dealings with the Church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sardica:
Sardica, a titular metropolitan see of Dacia Mediterranea, is modern Sofia, capital of Bulgaria. Its true name was Serdica, city of the Serdi, a Thracian people beaten by Crassus in 29 before Christ and subjected to Rome's client kingdom of Thrace. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia follows a Balkan city from tribe to metropolis.

When Thrace was suppressed in 49, the Serdi joined the Roman province of Thracia. Trajan raised their borough into the city of Ulpia Serdica. In 275 Aurelian moved Dacia's loyal soldiers and colonists south of the Danube, forming a new Dacia province that included Sardica. Diocletian later split that Dacia in two, and Sardica became civil and church metropolis of Dacia Mediterranea, with a mint under Gallienus.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sessa-aurunca:
Sessa Aurunca, a diocese in Campania in southern Italy, centers on a hill city in a fertile plain, whose large and beautiful cathedral dates to 1113. The Aurunci city became a Roman colony in 313 BC. It was the birthplace of the poet Lucilius and the philosopher Agostino Nifo. Local legend says Saint Peter himself preached the faith there.

The people honor as patron their bishop Saint Castus, martyred late in the third century, whose ancient basilica ruins still join to catacombs. The first bishop of certain date was Fortunatus in 499. Later bishops include Erveo, who served the city well, Pandulfo, who gave the cathedral its mosaic pulpit, and Galeazzo Florimonte, active in papal affairs under Paul III and Julius III.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-spalato-macar:
Spalato-Macarsca was a Dalmatian diocese, suffragan to Zara, rooted in the sacred ground of ancient Salona, where Titus, pupil of St. Paul, was said to have preached and the first martyrs shed their blood. This entry follows Salona's forty-seven known bishops, from Hesychius, mentioned by St. Augustine, through synods and disputes in which Gregory the Great took a deposed archdeacon's part.

Slavs destroyed Salona in 639, and Spalato rose from its ruins eight years later, its archbishops inheriting Salona's place after an eleven-year gap. Byzantine art under Justinian had already left its mark in Salona's baptistery and basilicas. And the entry gives readers an Adriatic church history written in stone as much as in documents.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-acca:
St. Acca, bishop of Hexham and patron of learning, lived from about 660 to 742, and this entry follows a Northumbrian who spent his life beside St. Wilfrid. Born into the household of Bosa, later bishop of York, Acca joined Wilfrid, perhaps as early as 678, travelled with him to Rome in 692. And, when Wilfrid regained Hexham, became abbot of St Andrew's monastery there, succeeding him as bishop after his death in 709.

Acca pressed on with finishing and adorning Wilfrid's churches, ruled his diocese and its worship with equal zeal. And brought the cantor Maban from Kent to teach the Roman chant handed down from St Gregory. Readers meet a bishop who treated learning, music, and building as one work.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-darerca:
Irish tradition remembers Darerca less for deeds of her own than for the remarkable family gathered around her. Sister of Patrick, Ireland's national apostle, she married twice and became mother to a host of saints, with some accounts crediting her with seventeen sons who all became bishops. This Catholic Encyclopedia entry of 1913 warns that medieval legend has thickly wrapped her real story, so firm facts are few.

Sorting tale from record, the piece names her husbands, Restitutus the Lombard and Chonas the Briton, and her children by each, including four bishops by Chonas and two sainted daughters. It follows Patrick's visit to Bredach, where he found three of her sons already serving as deacons. The entry suits readers tracing early Irish saints through family ties rather than through a single hero's life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-prisca:
Prisca, a martyr of the Roman Church, survives as a name tied to a catacomb, a church, and a title. Her dates are unknown, and her name is easily confused with Priscilla, wife of Aquila and pupil of Paul. A martyr Prisca's grave was venerated in the Catacomb of Priscilla on the Via Salaria, named in all seventh-century pilgrim itineraries.

A church of St Prisca stands on the Aventine, on the site of a very early title church mentioned in the fifth century. A bronze tablet found nearby in the eighteenth century, dated 224, granted citizenship to a senator named Caius Marius Pudens Cornelianus. The entry sifts names, graves, and stones, showing how little can be fixed about an early Roman martyr.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-veronica:
Veronica began not as a woman but as words: vera icon, the true image. In several regions a pious matron of Jerusalem is honoured who, one of the holy women walking with Jesus to Calvary, she gave him a cloth. His face stayed printed on it. She carried this image to Rome, where it was long exposed to public veneration.

Belief in authentic images of Christ connects with the old legend of Abgar of Edessa and the apocryphal Mors Pilati. To distinguish Rome's oldest and best known image it was called vera icon, and ordinary speech soon made that Veronica. By degrees popular imagination mistook the word for a person's name and attached legends to it. The entry traces how a phrase became a saint.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tarapaca:
Tarapacá is a Vicariate Apostolic in Chile, bounded by the Camarones canyon in the north and the Loa River in the south. It covers its civil province of 19,305 square miles. Its people include 106,215 Catholics and 3,821 non-Catholics. Eleven parishes hold sixty-three churches and chapels, served by thirty secular and fourteen regular priests.

Franciscans, Redemptorists, and Salesians hold four houses with twenty-four members. Sisters of the Good Shepherd, St Joseph of Cluny, and the Salesians hold five houses with fifty members. They run colleges, a hospital, an asylum, and a women's house of correction at Iquique. Erected in 1882 when Chile took the province from Peru, it has had five vicars. Yearly missions still reach the saltpetre workers, miners little given to religious practice.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thabraca:
Thabraca was a titular see of Numidia near the sea, between the Armua and the Tusca. It was the last Numidian city toward Zeugitana and a Roman colony. A road joined it to Simitthu, whose marbles it exported. At Thabraca, Gildo, brother of Firmus, killed himself. Under Genseric it held a monastery for men and one for women. Today it is Tabarka, in the civil district of Souk el-Arba, Tunis, a rather important fishing centre.

Facing it stands little Tabarca island, where the Genoese Lomellini kept a garrison from 1540 to 1742 on a coral-fishing grant from the Turks. Ruins of a stronghold, a church, and Genoese buildings still stand there. At Tabarka a pit used as a church survives, with Christian wall fragments, two Turkish fortresses, and cemeteries whose tombs bear mosaic covers. Bishops named include Victoricus at Carthage in 256, Rusticianus in 411, and Clarissimus in 646.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-slavs-in-:
Slavic newcomers to the United States and Canada, arriving in ever larger numbers, are counted and described here. Earliest arrivals predated the Civil War, but the past thirty years dwarfed earlier Irish and German waves. For two-thirds of that span no exact tongue or nationality figures were kept, only countries of origin, though the last twelve years brought better data.

Between 1899 and 1910 total immigration reached about ten million, of whom Slavs formed some 22 per cent, actually 2,117,240, besides native-born Slavs and earlier arrivals. Estimates put five and a half to six million Slavs in the United States. Peoples, churches, and settlements follow in a statistical portrait of a new America.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-united-st:
America's bounds, land, and people fill this enormous survey, opening with boundaries and area. Saint Croix River and a line to Saint John mark the east. The 45th parallel, Saint Lawrence, and Great Lakes mark the north. Rainy River and Lake of the Woods and the 49th parallel run westward to Puget Sound, then Juan de Fuca Strait, leaving Vancouver Island to Canada. Total area runs 3,026,789 square miles. 

Mississippi splits the country into unequal halves, flowing south from a lake below the 49th parallel. Atlantic, Gulf of Mexico, Rio Grande, and Pacific frame the rest. States, territories, population, races, religions, and church history follow in turn, making the entry a full geography and history of the republic at 1913.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thessalonica:
Macedonian metropolis Thessalonica, now Saloniki, is the great port city surveyed here. First a village called Alia near the Axius, now Vardar, it took the name Therma from hot springs east and south, and its gulf became the Thermaic Gulf. Xerxes's fleet sheltered there, Athenians held it in the Peloponnesian War, and Macedonian kings took it after Alexander's death.

Cassander enlarged the village, moved in folk from nearby towns, and named it for his wife Thessalonica. Rome's victory at Pydna in 168 before Christ made it capital of Macedonia's second district, and in 146 it became capital of the whole province. Paul's letters, Byzantine glory, and Ottoman rule carry the story to modern Saloniki, a crossroads of East and West.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thignica:
Numidian town Thignica, whose ruins are Ain Tounga southwest of Testour in Tunisia, is the Roman city described here. Rome's official list puts it in Numidia, though it truly lay in Proconsular Africa. Ruins sprawl over hilltops and slopes, vast and impressive. One inscription calls it Civitas Thignicensis, split in three parts, another records municipium rank early in the third century under the long name Septimium Aurelium Antoninianum Herculeum Frugiferum Thignica.

A Byzantine fort, trapezoid in shape with five square towers, stands near the centre, where an inscription names proconsul Domitius Zenophilus, 326 to 332, famous in Christian Africa's annals. Small triumphal arch, temple, Christian church, and enclosure walls complete the site. One bishop only is known: Aufidius, at Carthage in 411 against a Donatist rival.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tricca:
A titular see, suffragan of Larissa in Thessaly, set near the River Peneius on the Lethaeus, which devastated it in 1907. Homer names it as the kingdom of Machaon and Podaleirius, sons of Aesculapius and physicians of the Greek army. It held the oldest known temple of Aesculapius, found in 1902 with a pilgrims' hospital.

Socrates, Sozomenes and Nicephorus Callistus say Heliodorus, probably the author of the romance of Theagenes and Charicles, became Bishop of Tricca. A later sixth-century bishop, an Origenist and Monophysite, wrote a commentary on the Apocalypse wrongly published under another name. Latin titulars appear in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-university-of:
Salamanca began in the cathedral school, directed from the twelfth century by a magister scholarum, or chancellor. From that episcopal root, probably in 1230, sprang the royal foundation of Alfonso IX of León, who summoned the most experienced masters of sacred letters and set up schools. The foundation did not endure, and St Ferdinand stands as the real founder. On 6 April 1243 the saintly king took professors, students, and their property under his protection.

He granted them an ecclesiastical tribunal for settling disputes, and in his reign began the period of unrivalled brilliance that made Salamanca famed across Europe. The entry follows its colleges, its theologians and jurists, and its later decline and revival, giving a compact history of Spain's greatest medieval university and its enduring name.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-utica:
Utica was a titular see in Africa Proconsularis, founded by Tyrian colonists at the mouth of the Bagradas River near rich mines in 1110 before Christ, some 287 years before Carthage. It held two harbours, and in the Punic Wars it acted as Carthage's ally rather than its vassal. In 212 before Christ the Roman Ottacilius seized and plundered it.

After Carthage fell in 146 before Christ, Utica became capital of the Roman province of Africa and a free city, perhaps even tax-exempt. There Cato the Younger killed himself after defeat at Thapsus in 46 before Christ. Augustus granted citizenship to its people, and under Hadrian it became a colony. The entry follows its bishops and its later fate as a Christian see.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-vicariate-apo:
Athabasca is a vicariate apostolic in Canada's Northwest Territories, suffragan to St Boniface and erected in 1862 by Pius IX. It is bounded by Mackenzie to the north, Saskatchewan to the east and southeast, the 55th parallel to the south. The Rockies to the west, it was served entirely by Oblates of Mary Immaculate.

Its first vicar apostolic was Bishop Henri Faraud, succeeded by Bishop Emile Grouard, titular Bishop of Ibora. The mission counted eleven stations, twenty-three priests, twenty-eight Sisters of Providence, six Grey Nuns. About five thousand Catholics scattered across a vast northern territory where travel and climate made every station a feat of endurance.
doe-osti-2583249-grain2mesh-mesh-generat:
Report LA-UR-25-28367, by Keegan Davis of Los Alamos and issued August 13, 2025, introduces grain2mesh, a software package for building simulation meshes from images of granular materials. Rocks behave oddly under repeated loading, and the cause sits at the grain scale. Simulating grain interactions, shearing, cracking, and contrast between materials, first requires a mesh that faithfully copies the microstructure in a photograph or scan.

Image-based meshers often skip preprocessing, leaving jagged edges and distorted elements. In explicit solvers the smallest element sets the time step, so a few bad elements tax the whole run. Grain2mesh builds in noise reduction and lets users steer the process, checking fidelity before export. It writes the multi-phase mesh plus the input files finite element solvers need. Target uses include material fracturing, stress-strain analysis of natural and engineered materials, and nonlinear mesoscale studies.
doe-osti-2588031-science-of-scale-up-acc:
Andrew Wong, Sarah Baker, and Eric Duoss of Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, with Michael Resch and Volker Sick, wrote this workshop report, LLNL-RR-0069561, in August 2025. About fifty experts met in October 2024 to discuss chemical manufacturing scale-up. They came from universities, industry, national laboratories, and government. Their question: why do promising technologies stall between proof of concept and the market, and how can that climb be sped up?

The report distills seven critical themes for faster scale-up. Breakout sessions ground them in three technology families: electrochemical, thermochemical, and biological conversion processes. Electrochemical work needs durable materials above all, thermochemical work needs novel reactor designs and tighter supply chains, and biological work struggles with strain engineering and reactor design. Cross-cutting answers include interdisciplinary teams, steadier funding, and shared test facilities that cut the time, money, and risk each developer must carry alone.
doe-osti-3001948-american-wake-experimen:
Patrick Moriarty of the National Renewable Energy Laboratory and a multi lab team give the AWAKEN field campaign in DOE/SC-ARM-25-019, dated September 2025. AWAKEN, the American Wake Experiment, surrounded an Oklahoma wind farm with instruments to watch wakes. These are the long trails of slowed air behind turbines that sap the output of machines downwind. Wake losses are among the largest uncertainties in wind plant performance, and models have lacked a definitive dataset.

Scanners, lidars, radars and towers from the ARM programme and partners mapped flow through and around the plant across seasons. The campaign report covers background, notable events, headline results and the publication record already growing from the data. Future research opportunities point model developers to the open dataset. The volume is a campaign chronicle for the ARM community. It records what was deployed, what nature provided, and where the wake data now lives.
doe-osti-3002233-east-tennessee-technolo:
T. J. Mathews, R. T. Jett, N. A. Griffiths, P. G. Matson, and colleagues deliver a fiscal-year account in Oak Ridge report ORNL/SPR-2025/4073, dated September 2025. It covers the Biological Monitoring and Abatement Program at the East Tennessee Technology Park. The program watches fish and other aquatic life near the former K-25 site, where cleanup of past contamination continues. Living tissue shows exposure that water samples alone can miss.

Field crews sample on a set plan prepared for the Energy Department's Oak Ridge environmental office. Results are read against Tennessee water quality rules and the state's list of impaired waters. The yearly report tells regulators whether contamination is still reaching local streams and ponds. It also guides abatement steps, the actions taken to cut any exposure the sampling finds.
doe-osti-3011273-modeling-moisture-outga:
Moisture outgassing from silica filled silicones is cast into a single generalised kinetics model by McLean and Dinh of Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory in LLNL-TR-2014381. Total outgassing combines two parts. A dynamic vapour sorption part covers water diffusing out of the silicone matrix. A temperature programmed desorption part covers the first monolayers bound to silanol groups on the silica filler. A modified Page diffusion term carries the sorption part.

The model is applied to the silicones M9787 and LL50. Vacuum baked samples later re exposed to limited moisture are included. Where sorption data for baked material are absent, as received values serve as an upper limit approximation for the uptake term.
doe-osti-3012493-atmospheric-gases-as-qu:
Oak Ridge report ORNL/TM-2025/4393, by Jessica Weinberg, Thomas Mead, Melanie Mayes, and Christian Mark Salvador, dated January 2026, tests whether gases in the air can measure how urban a place is. The team tied the work to the urban heat island effect, the extra warmth cities hold compared with the land around them. Field measurements ran at two southeastern United States sites during the summer of 2025.

Instruments tracked inorganic gases nonstop, and volatile organic compounds were sampled every two weeks. The urban site averaged more carbon monoxide and nitrogen dioxide, at 878 and 17.99 parts per billion, against 796 and 12.46 at the rural site. The rural site instead showed more plant-made compounds such as isoprene. The contrast supports using air chemistry as a practical gauge of urbanization and heat island strength.
doe-osti-3012814-arctic-observing-experi:
Atmospheric Radiation Measurement report DOE/SC-ARM-26-002, by I. Rigor of the University of Washington and A. McCain of the U.S. National Ice Center, dated January 2026, reports on the Arctic Observing Experiment. The experiment grew out of a worry: temperature records from Arctic drifting buoys drive climate trend estimates, yet the instruments themselves had never been checked carefully against top-grade references.

In March 2013 the team deployed a suite of buoys beside the DOE ARM and NOAA climate sites in Barrow, Alaska. Readings there were compared with the reference stations for air temperature, ice surface temperature, pressure, and wind. Early results showed the color of a buoy's hull can bias its readings, since dark hulls warm in the sun. The report supports more accurate Arctic temperature trends.
doe-osti-3015563-east-tennessee-technolo:
ORNL/SPR-2026/4391 tracks wildlife contamination at a former uranium enrichment site. It is the East Tennessee Technology Park Biological Monitoring and Abatement Program report for calendar year 2025, dated January 2026. Crews sample fish and clams. Legacy pollution could move into food webs through them. Teresa Mathews led the author team.

At the K-901-A Pond, Asiatic clams deployed for monitoring are compared against reference clams from Little Sewee Creek. Total PCBs are the sum of Aroclors 1248, 1254, and 1260. The record runs from 1993 to 2025. In the K-720 Slough, monitored since 2009, largemouth bass are the target fish for fillet sampling. Full twenty-fish samples proved hard to collect. Common carp filled the count. The yearly report keeps the long trend lines unbroken for regulators.
doe-osti-3018744-scan2sim-software-to-co:
Adam J Beauchaine and Lee T Maccarone of Sandia describe their Scan2Sim software in SAND2026-16452R, revision 0, 2025. Testing an operational technology network safely means rebuilding it in simulation first. Doing that by hand is slow and error-prone. Scan2Sim automates the rebuild. It takes a detailed network scan as input. Out comes an instruction set that recreates the scanned network inside a virtualized emulation. Machine templates are picked by heuristic matching, which keeps the process fast.

The output targets Minimega, Sandia's own tool for repeatable experiment management. A typical run scans a subnet, such as a /24, and compiles the results into the emulation plan. Security evaluators gain a faithful copy of a plant network without touching the plant. Safety cases and attack exercises can then run on the copy. The report documents design and function for the teams who will operate it.
doe-osti-3023151-quantum-computing-algor:
Purdue University closes out award DE-SC0019215 with this final report on quantum computing for chemistry. Sabre Kais led the team at first, with Yong P Chen and Libai Huang as co-investigators, plus David Mazziotti and John Anderson at the University of Chicago. After 2024, Kais moved to NC State University and Huang took over as principal investigator. The target was coherent and strongly correlated chemical systems, which strain classical computers.

Work covered quantum algorithms for open quantum dynamics, shown on the Fenna-Matthews-Olson light-harvesting complex, a standard test case from photosynthesis research. Results went out through papers, lectures, and seminars at national meetings and universities. The report's products section lists the publications and patents the award produced, giving readers a map from the summary claims to the underlying studies.
doe-osti-3376850-section-3-reporting-pre:
Brookhaven National Laboratory report BNL-229895-2026-FORE, by A. McGovern of the Environmental Protection Division and dated July 2026, is the lab's Preserve America Section 3 account of its historic estate.
